segments.title: A hypothetical breakout under British colours west of Ireland
segments.body: One proposed alternative sends Bismarck and Prinz Eugen through the Faroes-Iceland gap and down the west coast of Ireland under British colours. The deception would depend on observers accepting them as a British battleship and cruiser without close inspection. The Irish Sea is rejected because its heavier shipping traffic would create more opportunities for discovery. A route west of Ireland would still be a major gamble, including the risk of Irish observers reporting the ships to Britain. The proposal assumes that apparent British identity might prevent such reports from attracting attention. It is a retrospective hypothetical made without the personal risks facing Lütjens. His own preference for Denmark Strait repeated a route he knew from Operation Berlin.

evidence.note: A hypothetical route west of Ireland under British colours, with identification, reporting, and hindsight limitations.
The Irish Sea is rejected because of its heavier shipping traffic.

segments.summary: An unexpected route west of Ireland under British colours offers a risky counterfactual, dependent on mistaken identification and the chance of escaping reports to Britain.

segments.title: How close was Rodney when her shells disabled Bismarck's turrets?
segments.body: The surviving track data does not provide one uncontested range for every hit. Rodney opened at roughly twenty-five thousand yards and continued closing throughout the action. By the period when individual Bismarck turrets were being picked off, the range had probably fallen below eighteen thousand yards, with estimates around sixteen to seventeen thousand. After the German main battery was disabled, Rodney approached to roughly three thousand yards. The mapped tracks become uncertain at points, so a precise single figure should not be treated as settled.

evidence.note: Rodney opened near 25,000 yards, probably disabled turrets below 18,000 yards, and later closed to roughly 3,000 yards.
A later estimate of approximately 16,000-17,000 yards is qualified by uncertainty about Rodney's plotted track.

segments.summary: Rodney opened around twenty-five thousand yards, was probably below eighteen thousand while disabling the main battery, and eventually closed to roughly three thousand yards.
segments.question: At what range was Rodney firing when her sixteen-inch salvos disabled Bismarck's turrets?
segments.answerShort: Probably around seventeen thousand yards, though the exact track is debated. Rodney began near twenty-five thousand yards and closed to about three thousand after Bismarck's main battery was out.

segments.title: Would sailing under British colours have made Bismarck a pirate?
segments.body: Sailing under another flag is distinguished here from attacking while displaying it. The proposed Bismarck deception would depend on changing colours before opening fire. Discovery would still expose the German ships to interception and battle. The proposal remains a risky hypothetical, with its legal distinction limited to the rule stated in this exchange.

evidence.note: Displaying another flag while sailing is distinguished from attacking under it; the proposed scheme is also treated as risky.

segments.summary: Sailing under British colours would not itself count as piracy in this account; attacking while displaying that flag would cross the stated boundary.
segments.question: Would disguising Bismarck as a British battleship with British colours have counted as piracy?
segments.answerShort: Sailing under British colours would not itself count as piracy in this account, provided the ship did not attack under that flag.

segments.title: Who could have ordered Bismarck's scuttling?
segments.body: The usual attribution of the scuttling order to Bismarck's first officer is questioned because several positions where he should have been stationed had been destroyed. That does not establish whether he was still alive or able to issue orders. A surviving senior engineering officer is offered as another possible source of the order. The destruction of command positions leaves the identity and sequence uncertain.

evidence.note: The conventional attribution to the first officer is questioned, with a surviving engineering officer offered as an alternative.

segments.summary: Destroyed command positions leave uncertainty over whether the first officer or a surviving engineering officer ordered the scuttling.
